chapters.title: Two cases: the Berlin train station ceiling and Snow's geese
Moral intuitions behind personality theory (Kant and Hegel)
Ten ways property supports human flourishing
The variants most relevant to artists
Moral rights in treaties and the US
Personality theory as the basis for moral rights
Open questions: imitation, alienability, and the Vanna White case
What personality theory is good for

key_points: Courts sided with artists whose works were altered after they were paid: von Gerkan's Berlin station ceiling had to be rebuilt, and the ribbons on Michael Snow's geese had to be removed.
Personality theory protects a psychic bond between artist and creation, rather than rewarding labor as fairness theory does.
Personality theory draws on Kant and Hegel: certain bonds with objects are crucial to human flourishing, so the law should protect them with property rights.
The lecture lists ten ways property supports flourishing, including peace of mind, privacy, autonomy, self-realization, security, responsibility, identity, civic virtue and self-expression.
Cartoonist Gary Larson asked fans not to post his cartoons online, calling them his children, illustrating self-expression and control over one's work.
The variants most relevant to artists are privacy, self-realization, identity and self-expression.

Continental European countries, most influenced by these ideas, grant moral rights: attribution, integrity, disclosure, withdrawal, protection against excessive criticism, and the droit de suite resale fee.
The Berne Convention requires attribution and integrity rights, but it lacks teeth and TRIPS doesn't incorporate them, so the US can largely avoid moral rights.
Because creativity is usually collaborative and builds on earlier works, some scholars argue personality theory supports more freedom for transformative uses.
Hard questions remain, such as whether artists can stop imitation, whether rights can be assigned, and whether a celebrity's persona deserves protection (the Vanna White robot ad case).
Personality theory doesn't give determinate answers; its value is to make us reflect on how control over creations affects self-fulfillment.

It suggests reforms: shorter copyright terms, rethinking employer ownership of employees' works, protecting independent artists, and broadening fair use, even at the cost of narrowing the integrity right.
